text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- The Swedish police force has attracted heavy critisism from the national audit office for breaing pension rules. Among other things it has paid out consulting fees to lift pensions.
- Fashion retailer Hennes & Mauritz (H&M) facees legal action by the Logg family on Friday for using the brand name L.O.G.G. on some of its clothes.

- Six companies, among them Saab/British aerospace, are fighting for a major order of 30 fighter planes from Hungary. At the end of May the companies will show their planes at an exhibition outside Budapest. Swedish aircraft maker Saab is held by Investor, the key holding company of the Wallenberg family.

- Sweden and several other European Union countries will recall their ambassadors from Iran, after Germany recalled its ambassador and called for fellow EU members to follow suit. Germany's decision derived from a German court ruling that Iran's political leaders ordered the killings of Kurdish opposition leaders in a 1992 Berlin attack.
- Sweden's drug police is calling for a register of mobile phone subscription owners to be able to track and bug people using the phones.
- Swedish compact disc sales fell two percent in the first quarter this year compared to the corresponding period a year earlier. March sales dropped eight percent from March 1996.

- The U.S. Court of Appeals has ruled in favour of Sweden's health care company Gambro in an important lawsuit against its U.S. competitor Baxter International. The court ruled that Gambro's patent is not invalid and that Baxter's dialysis machines infringe upon Gambro's patent.
- Scandinavian airline SAS is moving towards the final stage of deciding whether Airbus or Boeing will win an order worth about 10 billion crowns for about 15 aircraft.

- The efforts of SAS to trim costs and boost productivity had an impact in the first quarter of the year. "In terms of traffic volumes SAS had a decent first quarter," SAS chief executive Jan Stenberg was quoted as saying. "I feel that one can already see the result of our efforts to increase productivity and become more cost effective." SAS is due to release first quarter earnings on May 6.

- There seems to be a lack of fresh ideas in Sweden's large corporations. This is a conclusion which can be drawn from the recently announced plans of construction group Skanska, engineer Sandvik and vehicle maker Volvo to transfer about 20 billion crowns worth of capital to shareholders, the newspaper's stock analyst said.
